A1.justification: Both PDFs describe emg2speech and retain identifiable methods and experiments. All pages, equations, figures, and tables are readable. V1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–D, which were included in the comparison.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.3 report original gesture-clustering results, speech-representation correlations, and unit and phoneme decoding experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds ALS decoding, phoneme-guided training, human intelligibility and quality ratings, and additional empirical analyses in the appendices.

M1.justification: V1 lists phoneme-guided decoding as future work. V2 Section 5.3.1 and Appendix B implement dual CTC prediction heads, a GRU-derived unit-to-phoneme probability table, and a consistency loss. Appendix D.4 also introduces an EMG-to-text pipeline using a pronunciation lexicon, language model, and WFST decoder.

E1.justification: V2 retains the healthy speech and 12-participant gesture datasets under explicit names and adds DATA_ALS: approximately one hour of silent articulation from an ALS participant, covering 600 sentences and roughly 300 words. Appendix D.4 adds word-level EMG-to-text evaluation and uses LibriSpeech-100 transcripts to construct its decoder.

E2.justification: The main covariance, diagonal-power, and spectrogram comparators remain. Appendix D.4/Table 6 adds an evaluated EMG2TEXT alternative to direct EMG2SPEECH. Section 5.2 omits v1's audio-spectrogram-to-EMG-spectrogram probe, reported at r = 0.37. Appendix C's expanded literature comparisons are contextual citations rather than newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The healthy corpus's reported training/validation/test split changes from 7000/1000/1660 to 8500/760/400 sentences. V2 adds the ALS split of 500/40/60, human transcription by three raters across all 460 test utterances, MOS evaluation by ten raters on 35 utterances, and training-size experiments with fixed validation/test splits.

E4.justification: V2 adds CTC-only versus phoneme-guided training comparisons, analysis of unit-to-phoneme associations (Figure 6), a training-size ablation (Figure 7), training/validation loss analysis (Figure 8), and human transcription error distributions (Figure 9). These substantially extend the retained feature comparisons and layer-wise probes.

E5.justification: V1 Tables 1–2 already contain plus/minus values without specifying seed counts. V2 Tables 1–4 explicitly report averages over five random seeds, and Table 3 adds p < 10^-6 for phoneme-guided training. V2 also reports cross-rater variability. The PDFs do not establish an increase from a known previous run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 contain replacement results under the revised split: full-covariance UER changes from 58.7% to 56.08%, and PER from 41.42% to 32.78%. Gesture-power clustering accuracy changes from 70.6% to 61.41%, with chance corrected from 10% to 7.69%. New results include phoneme-guided UERs of 51.81%/46.98%, human WERs of 62.55%/50.82% for healthy/ALS data, and MOS 3.79.

T1.justification: Appendix B introduces mathematical definitions for the unit-conditioned phoneme table, posterior marginalization, consistency loss, and combined training objective. The existing covariance geometry and linear-probing formulation remain substantively unchanged. The additions formalize the new method without introducing theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and new Section 2.1 add silent-speech synthesis in ALS, operation with approximately 40 minutes of training data, and phoneme-guided synthesis as central contributions. V1's speculative few-shot/zero-shot potential statement disappears. The central claim linking EMG power to self-supervised speech representations remains.

C2.justification: New Section 7 acknowledges single-participant clinical evidence, untested day-to-day shifts, and absent long-term validation. Appendices B–D add interpretations of phonetic associations, data-limited learning, and EMG-to-text tradeoffs. V2 also explains how perceptually plausible synthesized speech can coexist with high linguistic error rates and qualifies cross-study performance comparisons.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents transcript-derived gTTS targets, the separate use of recorded audio for probing, channel normalization, detailed TDS architecture, loss weights, and the 50-epoch AdamW schedule. It supplies code/data/project links and states resource release, replacing v1's future-availability footnote. These are substantial disclosure gains; unspecified v1 details do not establish underlying procedure changes.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix C substantially expand positioning against earlier EMG and invasive speech interfaces, including Benster et al. (2024), with detailed distinctions concerning alignment, vocabularies, streaming, and evaluation comparability. Additional references support longitudinal stability, covariance geometry, language-model decoding, and perceptual evaluation.

P1.justification: V2 extensively revises prose and reorganizes existing material: gesture acquisition moves into Data, recording details move to Appendix A, and Continuing Work is replaced by Conclusion and Limitations. It adds a contributions subsection and separate dataset/result subsections, changes SS terminology to S3, and renames the rotation-invariance module shift-tolerant.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Existing figures are resized and renumbered, with electrode photographs moved to Appendix A. Tables 1–2 gain feature-dimension columns, while new Tables 3–6 and Figures 6–10 present the additional comparisons and analyses. Correlation-figure captions also clarify the quantities compared.

improvement.justification: V1 left phoneme-guided decoding and assessment of generated audio as continuing work. V2 implements that method, adds full-test-set human intelligibility evaluation and sampled MOS ratings, demonstrates silent articulation in ALS, and substantially improves implementation and access documentation. These additions resolve important gaps in validating and reproducing the synthesis claim. High WER, one ALS participant, and revised data splits still limit clinical and cross-version performance conclusions.
